rules.quote: Write clear page titles.
rules.specification: Interpret clarity as identifying the page’s topic or purpose, rather than imposing an unstated title-length limit.
rules.violation_condition: A page title does not clearly identify the page’s topic or purpose.
rules.why: G-1: title clarity is a distinct textual requirement in the accessibility fundamentals.

rules.quote: This is the first topic a screen reader user will hear and should align with the first heading on the page.
rules.specification: ‘This’ refers to the page title. Interpret ‘align’ as agreement in topic or purpose, not a requirement for identical wording.
rules.violation_condition: The page title and the first heading identify different topics or purposes.
rules.why: G-1: alignment with the first heading is independent of whether the title itself is clear.

covers.quote: Organise content using clear heading levels.
use headings to chunk information so it works well on screen for the user.

rules.quote: Organise content with a clear structure using section headings.
rules.violation_condition: Content containing distinct sections lacks section headings that expose its structure.
when: Applies where the content has distinct sections to organise.
rules.why: G-4: consolidate the instructions to expose content structure through section headings.

covers.quote: Clear headings are specific to the topic they describe.
Clearly describe the topics or the following section in the headings.
Write headings that tell the user what is in the content below it.
Headings should state the main point.
Use words that accurately describe the content.
Don’t use empty words or phrases (for example, ‘more’ or ‘related information’).
Only include information in the section that is relevant to the heading.

rules.quote: State the main point
rules.violation_condition: A heading is empty or generic, fails to identify the main point of its section, or does not accurately represent the information grouped under it.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: specificity, non-empty wording and heading–content relevance are cases of one semantic-fit check.

covers.quote: Keep them brief.
Write headings that are no more than 70 characters (including spaces).

rules.quote: Use 70 characters or fewer
rules.violation_condition: A heading contains more than 70 characters, counting spaces.
when: Include spaces in the character count.
rules.why: G-4: the explicit character limit operationalises the instruction to keep headings brief.

rules.quote: Avoid questions as headings
rules.violation_condition: A heading is phrased as a question.
rules.why: G-1: question form is a distinct check; the following paragraphs explain its rationale.

covers.quote: Begin each heading with keywords and keep it to the point.
Start headings and subheadings with keywords that help people to make a connection.
The keywords should relate to the main content below the heading.

parts.quote: Write a heading starting with the main keywords

rules.quote: Use keywords to start headings
rules.violation_condition: The meaningful keywords for the section occur late in its heading rather than at the start.
when: The opening keywords should relate to the main content below the heading.
The first 2 or 3 words are particularly important.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: keyword relevance and placement qualify one frontloading check.

rules.quote: Keep each section concise
rules.specification: The page gives no length threshold for a concise section. The 70-character limit applies to headings, not sections.
rules.violation_condition: A section is unnecessarily long or diffuse rather than concise.
rules.why: G-1 and E-4: section concision is distinct from heading length; do not invent a numerical section limit.

covers.quote: Write headings in a complete organised hierarchy.

rules.quote: Don’t skip heading levels
rules.violation_condition: A heading introduces a deeper subsection without the intervening parent heading level, such as moving directly from level 1 to level 3.
when: Check transitions into deeper heading levels.
Returning from a deeper level to a higher-level heading does not require intervening headings.
rules.why: G-4: a complete hierarchy and not skipping levels express the same structural check.

covers.quote: Use one level 1 heading

rules.quote: Use just one level 1 heading per webpage.
rules.violation_condition: A webpage has a level 1 heading count other than one.
when: The one-heading restriction is for webpages, not the main sections of printed documents.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: use the body’s explicit webpage scope and keep heading cardinality as one check.

rules.quote: Make it unique to your site.
rules.violation_condition: A webpage’s level 1 heading duplicates the level 1 heading of another page on the same site.
when: Compare the level 1 heading with those on other pages of the same site.
rules.why: G-1: site-wide uniqueness is independent of the number of level 1 headings on a page.

covers.quote: If no guidelines apply, use a ‘Heading 1’ style for the main sections in the document.

rules.quote: In documents, use level 1 headings (or ‘Heading 1’ style) for the main sections, such as part titles.
rules.violation_condition: A main section in a printed document is assigned a heading level or style other than level 1 or ‘Heading 1’, without an applicable organisational convention.
when: Applies to printed documents.
The later print guidance makes this the default when no organisational heading guidelines apply.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: consolidate the repeated print convention and its organisational-guideline condition.

covers.quote: Make the headings relate

rules.quote: Every heading and subheading must relate to the heading above it so the grouping of information is logical and clear for users.
rules.violation_condition: A subordinate heading is not logically related to its parent heading.
when: ‘The heading above it’ means the parent in the hierarchy, rather than merely the preceding sibling heading.
rules.why: G-4: the body states the relationship requirement and explicitly makes it mandatory.

covers.quote: Try to use only 3 or 4 heading levels at the most.
You can use deeper heading levels (level 4 and below) for very complex documents, but try to avoid it.

rules.quote: Avoid level 5 and deeper heading levels
rules.specification: Use level 5 as the discouraged-depth boundary, following the heading and the stated maximum of 3 or 4 levels. The following reference to deeper levels beginning at level 4 is not fully consistent with that boundary.
rules.violation_condition: A document uses level 5 or deeper headings without the need for a very complex hierarchy.
when: Very complex documents may use deeper levels, although the page still recommends avoiding them.
rules.why: G-2, G-3 and E-4: keep the depth recommendation and complex-document permission together, exposing the boundary ambiguity.

covers.quote: Separate each heading from the next one by some text, even if it’s only a sentence.

rules.quote: Space out headings
rules.violation_condition: Two successive headings have no explanatory text between them.
when: Even a single sentence between headings is sufficient.
rules.why: G-4: the body resolves ‘space out’ as intervening text, not visual spacing.

covers.quote: Give each heading level in a section at least one other heading at the same level.

examples.note: The complete list is one example under ‘Like this’.

parts.quote: H1: Apply for a drivers licence

examples.note: The complete list is one example under ‘Not this’; it also contains other hierarchy problems.

rules.quote: Create at least 2 headings for each level
rules.specification: Count sibling headings within their parent section. Exempt the single level 1 webpage title, consistent with the explicit one-level-1 rule and the compliant example.
rules.violation_condition: A section contains a subordinate heading level with only one heading at that level.
when: Does not require a second level 1 title on a webpage.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: one sibling-count check, with the single webpage title exception made explicit.

covers.quote: Use numbered headings only when they relate to a series of steps.
In print, you can use numbered headings to help people cross-reference information:

rules.quote: Use numbered headings only for steps
rules.violation_condition: Numbered headings organise material that is not a series of steps, except where numbering supports cross-references in print.
when: Numbering is appropriate for headings that relate to a series of steps.
In print, numbered headings may also support cross-references.
rules.why: G-2, G-3 and G-4: the print permission relaxes the steps-only rule rather than creating a separate rule.

covers.quote: Don’t use numbered headings in the preliminary pages or endmatter in a report.

rules.quote: If you use numbered headings, use them only in the body.
rules.violation_condition: A printed document has numbered headings outside its body, including preliminary pages or endmatter.
when: Applies to numbered headings in print.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: preliminary pages and endmatter are cases of the same outside-the-body prohibition.

rules.quote: Don’t number more than the first 3 heading levels.
rules.violation_condition: A level 4 or deeper heading in a printed document is numbered.
when: Applies to numbered headings in print.
rules.why: G-1: numbering depth is distinct from whether numbering is appropriate and where it appears.

covers.quote: They should have the same:
grammatical form (called ‘parallel structure’).

rules.quote: Be consistent: use a parallel structure
rules.violation_condition: Headings at the same level use inconsistent grammatical forms, such as mixing noun phrases and instructions.
when: Compare headings at the same level.
rules.why: G-1: grammatical parallelism is a distinct check from consistency of the headings’ overall message.

covers.quote: All headings in a level should be consistent.
They should have the same:

rules.quote: overall message (for example, they are all steps in a process)
rules.violation_condition: Headings at the same level serve inconsistent kinds of message, rather than a consistent organising purpose.
when: Compare headings at the same level; all being steps in a process is one example of consistency.
rules.why: G-1: the list’s normative lead-in requires message consistency independently of grammatical parallelism.

covers.quote: Format headings so the heading levels are visibly different.
People should be able to tell the difference between heading levels at a glance.

rules.quote: Use unique formatting for each level of heading
rules.violation_condition: Different heading levels have formatting that does not make their levels visibly distinguishable.
rules.why: G-4: consolidate the heading and its two statements of visible differentiation.

rules.quote: don’t rely on colour as the only way to differentiate heading levels
rules.violation_condition: Colour is the sole formatting distinction between heading levels.
when: Colour may supplement other distinctions between heading levels.
rules.why: G-1: colour-only differentiation can violate this rule even when levels look different to some readers.

covers.quote: Don’t add an underline

rules.quote: Don’t underline headings or any other text.
rules.specification: Interpret this as a prohibition on added underline formatting, not on the conventional underline identifying a genuine hyperlink.
rules.violation_condition: A heading or other text has added underline formatting.
rules.why: G-4: use the body because it explicitly extends the prohibition beyond headings.

covers.quote: Apply HTML elements, tags and styles to headings
Use the correct HTML element for the heading level.
Apply correct inbuilt heading styles so they can be automatically added to navigation and contents pages.

examples.note: The lead-in and list form one example of heading-level elements.

parts.quote: A page about paying your tax might use these headings:
H1 = ‘Lodging your tax return’ (the page title)
H2 = ‘Individual tax return’ (a heading for a main section)

rules.quote: Use styles, tags and HTML elements to identify headings in digital content.
rules.violation_condition: A digital heading lacks semantic heading markup or a built-in heading style, or its element or style identifies the wrong heading level.
when: Applies to digital content.
Use the HTML element or built-in heading style appropriate to the heading level.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: HTML elements and built-in styles are format-specific ways to identify headings and their levels.

rules.quote: If your organisation uses templates, use the template styles.
rules.violation_condition: A document produced under an organisational template uses heading styles other than the template’s styles.
when: Applies when the organisation uses templates.
rules.why: G-2: the organisational-template condition limits a checkable property of the document’s heading styles.

rules.quote: The title of a document uses the ‘Title’ style.
rules.violation_condition: A printed document’s title uses a style other than ‘Title’ when no organisational heading guidelines apply.
when: Applies to printed documents.
Use this default when no organisational heading guidelines apply.
rules.why: G-1 and G-2: the title-style convention is distinct from the main-section heading convention and shares its default-style context.

covers.quote: This means you should use a capital letter only for:
the first letter of the first word
the first letter of any proper nouns
letters in acronyms and initialisms.
Don’t write headings in all capital letters as users could misread words.
If you work for an organisation that uses all capitals for headings, make sure any abbreviations are easy to understand.

rules.quote: Use sentence case for headings to help people read the text more easily.
rules.specification: Treat organisation-required all-capital headings as an exception acknowledged by the following paragraph. Otherwise apply sentence case.
rules.violation_condition: A heading capitalises ordinary words beyond the first word, including title case or all capitals, without a proper-name, acronym, initialism or acknowledged organisational exception.
when: Capitalise the first letter of the first word.
Retain capitals required by proper nouns, acronyms and initialisms.
The page acknowledges organisations that use all capitals for headings.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: sentence case, capitalisation exceptions and the all-capital warning belong to one capitalisation check.

covers.quote: Even if the heading is a sentence, it doesn’t need a full stop at the end.

rules.quote: Don’t use a full stop to end headings
rules.violation_condition: A heading ends with a sentence-ending full stop.
when: Applies even when the heading is a complete sentence.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: sentence headings are explicitly included in the same terminal-punctuation check.

covers.quote: Don’t use a shortened form in a heading unless it is better known than the full term (for example, ‘DNA’ and ‘CSIRO’).
If you work for an organisation that uses all capitals for headings, make sure any abbreviations are easy to understand.

rules.quote: Avoid using shortened forms in headings
rules.specification: Assess familiarity and clarity for the intended audience. The page explicitly permits better-known forms such as DNA and CSIRO and separately requires understandable abbreviations in organisational all-capital headings.
rules.violation_condition: A heading contains a shortened form that is not better known than its full term, or an abbreviation whose meaning is unclear in an organisation-required all-capital heading.
when: A shortened form is allowed when it is better known than the full term.
Abbreviations in organisation-required all-capital headings must remain easy to understand.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: keep the familiarity exception and all-capital abbreviation condition with the shortened-form check.

anchor.quote: Write clear page titles.
anchor.suffix: This is the first topic a scree

tags.specification: Interpret clarity as identifying the page’s topic or purpose, rather than imposing an unstated title-length limit.
tags.violation_condition: A page title does not clearly identify the page’s topic or purpose.

rules.why: G-1: title clarity is a distinct textual requirement in the accessibility fundamentals.

anchor.quote: This is the first topic a screen reader user will hear and should align with the first heading on the page.

tags.specification: ‘This’ refers to the page title. Interpret ‘align’ as agreement in topic or purpose, not a requirement for identical wording.
tags.violation_condition: The page title and the first heading identify different topics or purposes.

rules.why: G-1: alignment with the first heading is independent of whether the title itself is clear.

anchor.suffix: Clearly describe the topics or

covers.prefix: ontent and find what they need.
covers.quote: Organise content using clear heading levels.
use headings to chunk information so it works well on screen for the user.

tags.violation_condition: Content containing distinct sections lacks section headings that expose its structure.

when: Applies where the content has distinct sections to organise.
rules.why: G-4: consolidate the instructions to expose content structure through section headings.

anchor.quote: State the main point

covers.quote: Clear headings are specific to the topic they describe.
Clearly describe the topics or the following section in the headings.
Write headings that tell the user what is in the content below it.
Headings should state the main point.
covers.suffix: This helps users find and use c

covers.quote: Use words that accurately describe the content.
covers.suffix: Don’t use empty words or phrase

covers.quote: Don’t use empty words or phrases (for example, ‘more’ or ‘related information’).
Only include information in the section that is relevant to the heading.

tags.violation_condition: A heading is empty or generic, fails to identify the main point of its section, or does not accurately represent the information grouped under it.

rules.why: G-2 and G-4: specificity, non-empty wording and heading–content relevance are cases of one semantic-fit check.

anchor.quote: Use 70 characters or fewer

covers.quote: Keep them brief.
covers.suffix: They are signposts for people a

covers.quote: Write headings that are no more than 70 characters (including spaces).

tags.violation_condition: A heading contains more than 70 characters, counting spaces.

when: Include spaces in the character count.
rules.why: G-4: the explicit character limit operationalises the instruction to keep headings brief.

anchor.quote: Avoid questions as headings

tags.violation_condition: A heading is phrased as a question.

rules.why: G-1: question form is a distinct check; the following paragraphs explain its rationale.

anchor.quote: Use keywords to start headings

covers.quote: Begin each heading with keywords and keep it to the point.
Start headings and subheadings with keywords that help people to make a connection.
The keywords should relate to the main content below the heading.
covers.suffix: Pay special attention to the fi

parts.quote: Write a heading starting with the main keywords

tags.violation_condition: The meaningful keywords for the section occur late in its heading rather than at the start.

when: The opening keywords should relate to the main content below the heading.
The first 2 or 3 words are particularly important.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: keyword relevance and placement qualify one frontloading check.

anchor.quote: Keep each section concise
anchor.suffix: and use headings to chunk infor

tags.specification: The page gives no length threshold for a concise section. The 70-character limit applies to headings, not sections.
tags.violation_condition: A section is unnecessarily long or diffuse rather than concise.

rules.why: G-1 and E-4: section concision is distinct from heading length; do not invent a numerical section limit.

anchor.quote: Don’t skip heading levels

covers.quote: Write headings in a complete organised hierarchy.

tags.violation_condition: A heading introduces a deeper subsection without the intervening parent heading level, such as moving directly from level 1 to level 3.

when: Check transitions into deeper heading levels.
Returning from a deeper level to a higher-level heading does not require intervening headings.
rules.why: G-4: a complete hierarchy and not skipping levels express the same structural check.

anchor.quote: Use just one level 1 heading per webpage.
anchor.suffix: Make it unique to your site. Th

covers.quote: Use one level 1 heading

tags.violation_condition: A webpage has a level 1 heading count other than one.

when: The one-heading restriction is for webpages, not the main sections of printed documents.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: use the body’s explicit webpage scope and keep heading cardinality as one check.

anchor.quote: Make it unique to your site.
anchor.suffix: This helps users understand the

tags.violation_condition: A webpage’s level 1 heading duplicates the level 1 heading of another page on the same site.

when: Compare the level 1 heading with those on other pages of the same site.
rules.why: G-1: site-wide uniqueness is independent of the number of level 1 headings on a page.

anchor.quote: In documents, use level 1 headings (or ‘Heading 1’ style) for the main sections, such as part titles.

covers.quote: If no guidelines apply, use a ‘Heading 1’ style for the main sections in the document.
covers.suffix: The title of a document uses th

tags.violation_condition: A main section in a printed document is assigned a heading level or style other than level 1 or ‘Heading 1’, without an applicable organisational convention.

when: Applies to printed documents.
The later print guidance makes this the default when no organisational heading guidelines apply.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: consolidate the repeated print convention and its organisational-guideline condition.

anchor.quote: Every heading and subheading must relate to the heading above it so the grouping of information is logical and clear for users.

covers.quote: Make the headings relate

tags.violation_condition: A subordinate heading is not logically related to its parent heading.

when: ‘The heading above it’ means the parent in the hierarchy, rather than merely the preceding sibling heading.
rules.why: G-4: the body states the relationship requirement and explicitly makes it mandatory.

anchor.quote: Avoid level 5 and deeper heading levels

covers.quote: Try to use only 3 or 4 heading levels at the most.
covers.suffix: A simpler structure is easier t

covers.quote: You can use deeper heading levels (level 4 and below) for very complex documents, but try to avoid it.

tags.specification: Use level 5 as the discouraged-depth boundary, following the heading and the stated maximum of 3 or 4 levels. The following reference to deeper levels beginning at level 4 is not fully consistent with that boundary.
tags.violation_condition: A document uses level 5 or deeper headings without the need for a very complex hierarchy.

when: Very complex documents may use deeper levels, although the page still recommends avoiding them.
rules.why: G-2, G-3 and E-4: keep the depth recommendation and complex-document permission together, exposing the boundary ambiguity.

anchor.quote: Space out headings

covers.quote: Separate each heading from the next one by some text, even if it’s only a sentence.
covers.suffix: This helps create a clear disti

tags.violation_condition: Two successive headings have no explanatory text between them.

when: Even a single sentence between headings is sufficient.
rules.why: G-4: the body resolves ‘space out’ as intervening text, not visual spacing.

anchor.quote: Create at least 2 headings for each level

covers.quote: Give each heading level in a section at least one other heading at the same level.
covers.suffix: This avoids the appearance of s

examples.note: The complete list is one example under ‘Like this’.

parts.quote: H1: Apply for a drivers licence

examples.note: The complete list is one example under ‘Not this’; it also contains other hierarchy problems.

tags.specification: Count sibling headings within their parent section. Exempt the single level 1 webpage title, consistent with the explicit one-level-1 rule and the compliant example.
tags.violation_condition: A section contains a subordinate heading level with only one heading at that level.

when: Does not require a second level 1 title on a webpage.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: one sibling-count check, with the single webpage title exception made explicit.

anchor.quote: Use numbered headings only for steps

covers.quote: Use numbered headings only when they relate to a series of steps.
In print, you can use numbered headings to help people cross-reference information:

tags.violation_condition: Numbered headings organise material that is not a series of steps, except where numbering supports cross-references in print.

when: Numbering is appropriate for headings that relate to a series of steps.
In print, numbered headings may also support cross-references.
rules.why: G-2, G-3 and G-4: the print permission relaxes the steps-only rule rather than creating a separate rule.

anchor.quote: If you use numbered headings, use them only in the body.

covers.quote: Don’t use numbered headings in the preliminary pages or endmatter in a report.

tags.violation_condition: A printed document has numbered headings outside its body, including preliminary pages or endmatter.

when: Applies to numbered headings in print.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: preliminary pages and endmatter are cases of the same outside-the-body prohibition.

anchor.quote: Don’t number more than the first 3 heading levels.

tags.violation_condition: A level 4 or deeper heading in a printed document is numbered.

when: Applies to numbered headings in print.
rules.why: G-1: numbering depth is distinct from whether numbering is appropriate and where it appears.

anchor.quote: Be consistent: use a parallel structure

covers.quote: They should have the same:
grammatical form (called ‘parallel structure’).

tags.violation_condition: Headings at the same level use inconsistent grammatical forms, such as mixing noun phrases and instructions.

when: Compare headings at the same level.
rules.why: G-1: grammatical parallelism is a distinct check from consistency of the headings’ overall message.

anchor.quote: overall message (for example, they are all steps in a process)

covers.quote: All headings in a level should be consistent.
They should have the same:

tags.violation_condition: Headings at the same level serve inconsistent kinds of message, rather than a consistent organising purpose.

when: Compare headings at the same level; all being steps in a process is one example of consistency.
rules.why: G-1: the list’s normative lead-in requires message consistency independently of grammatical parallelism.

anchor.quote: Use unique formatting for each level of heading

covers.quote: Format headings so the heading levels are visibly different.
covers.suffix: This helps users scan the text.

covers.quote: People should be able to tell the difference between heading levels at a glance.

tags.violation_condition: Different heading levels have formatting that does not make their levels visibly distinguishable.

rules.why: G-4: consolidate the heading and its two statements of visible differentiation.

anchor.quote: don’t rely on colour as the only way to differentiate heading levels

tags.violation_condition: Colour is the sole formatting distinction between heading levels.

when: Colour may supplement other distinctions between heading levels.
rules.why: G-1: colour-only differentiation can violate this rule even when levels look different to some readers.

anchor.quote: Don’t underline headings or any other text.

covers.quote: Don’t add an underline

tags.specification: Interpret this as a prohibition on added underline formatting, not on the conventional underline identifying a genuine hyperlink.
tags.violation_condition: A heading or other text has added underline formatting.

rules.why: G-4: use the body because it explicitly extends the prohibition beyond headings.

anchor.quote: Use styles, tags and HTML elements to identify headings in digital content.

covers.quote: Apply HTML elements, tags and styles to headings

Apply correct inbuilt heading styles so they can be automatically added to navigation and contents pages.

tags.violation_condition: A digital heading lacks semantic heading markup or a built-in heading style, or its element or style identifies the wrong heading level.

when: Applies to digital content.
Use the HTML element or built-in heading style appropriate to the heading level.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: HTML elements and built-in styles are format-specific ways to identify headings and their levels.

anchor.quote: If your organisation uses templates, use the template styles.
